content: Physical activity offers significant health benefits for adults and older adults living with chronic conditions, including cancer survivors, individuals with hypertension, type 2 diabetes, and those living with HIV. For cancer survivors, engaging in physical activity reduces all-cause mortality, cancer-specific mortality, and the risk of cancer recurrence or secondary cancers. For individuals with hypertension, physical activity improves cardiovascular disease mortality, slows disease progression, enhances physical function, and improves health-related quality of life. In people with type 2 diabetes, physical activity lowers cardiovascular disease mortality and slows disease progression. For individuals living with HIV, physical activity improves physical fitness and mental health by reducing symptoms of anxiety and depression, without negatively affecting disease progression (e.g., CD4 count or viral load) or body composition. Adults with chronic conditions should aim to engage in physical activity according to their abilities, even if they cannot meet the recommended levels. Starting with small amounts of physical activity and gradually increasing the frequency, intensity, and duration over time is advised. Consulting a healthcare professional or physical activity specialist can help tailor activity plans to individual needs, abilities, limitations, medications, and treatment plans. Pre-exercise medical clearance is generally unnecessary for lightto moderate-intensity activities, such as brisk walking, unless contraindications exist. Higher levels of sedentary behavior in adults, including those with chronic conditions, are associated with poor health outcomes such as increased all-cause mortality, cardiovascular disease mortality, cancer mortality, and the incidence of cardiovascular disease, cancer, and type 2 diabetes. Adults should aim to replace sedentary time with physical activity of any intensity, as even light-intensity activity provides health benefits. For children and adolescents living with disabilities, physical activity offers similar health benefits as for their peers without disabilities. Engaging in at least 60 minutes of moderateto vigorous-intensity aerobic physical activity daily, with activities that strengthen muscles and bones at least three times per week, is recommended. Limiting sedentary behavior, particularly recreational screen time, is also advised. Starting with small amounts of activity and gradually increasing intensity and duration is beneficial. The health benefits of physical activity outweigh the risks when it is appropriate to the individual’s current activity level, health status, and physical function. For adults living with disabilities, physical activity improves physical function, mental health, and quality of life. Specific benefits include improved physical and cognitive function in individuals with conditions such as multiple sclerosis, spinal cord injury, Parkinson’s disease, stroke, schizophrenia, intellectual disabilities, and major clinical depression. Adults with disabilities should aim for at least 150–300 minutes of moderate-intensity aerobic activity or 75–150 minutes of vigorous-intensity aerobic activity weekly, along with muscle-strengthening activities involving all major muscle groups on two or more days per week. Older adults with disabilities should also include multicomponent physical activities emphasizing balance and strength training at least three days per week to enhance functional capacity and prevent falls. Globally, physical inactivity is a leading contributor to mortality, with an estimated 4–5 million deaths per year potentially preventable if populations were more active. Physical activity is a protective factor against noncommunicable diseases such as cardiovascular disease, type 2 diabetes, and certain cancers, and it also benefits mental health, delays dementia onset, and supports healthy weight maintenance. Sedentary behavior, defined as low-energy activities performed while sitting, reclining, or lying down, is associated with increased risks of cardiovascular disease, type 2 diabetes, and mortality. The World Health Organization (WHO) emphasizes the importance of physical activity across all age groups and populations, including those with chronic conditions and disabilities. Updated guidelines provide evidence-based recommendations tailored to specific subpopulations, aiming to reduce health inequities and promote physical activity globally. These guidelines align with the WHO Global Action Plan on Physical Activity 2018–2030, which seeks to reduce physical inactivity by 15% by 2030.
